passage:
"Santosh, Rohit's at the gate. Cricket?"
"Not today, Amma."
"That's the fourth time this month. What's going on? Always sulking in this dark room."
"I'm not sulking. My head hurts."
"Again? It's nothing, kanna. Drink water, you'll be fine."
"You always say it's nothing! It's behind my eyes, almost every day after school. I can't even read the board without squinting."
"Every day?"
"Most days. I stopped telling you because you'd just say drink water."
"Lavanya, come here. Listen to your brother."
"Anna, why didn't you tell me? You've been snapping at everyone."
"Because nobody believes me."
"I believe you. I'm sorry, Santosh. Tomorrow we'll go to Dr. Menon, and get your eyes checked too."
"Really?"
"Really. And no cricket until we know. Just rest."

qa.q: How often does Santosh say his head hurts?
qa.a: Most days, behind his eyes, after school.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when Amma said it was nothing?
qa.a: He felt hurt and misunderstood, as if nobody believed him, which is why he had stopped telling anyone.

qa.q: What changed once Amma took him seriously?
qa.a: She believed him, apologised and planned a proper check with the doctor and an eye test, which eased the weight he had been carrying alone.

qa.q: How had Lavanya experienced Santosh's moods?
qa.a: Lavanya had seen him snapping at everyone without knowing he was in pain, and wished he had told her.

grounding: Shows a teenager with frequent headaches seeming moody and avoiding plans, feeling dismissed, and relieved once believed and taken for a check.

passage: Last year I became the friend who always cancelled. I'm Urmila, and for about four months I had headaches almost every afternoon, a tight band round my forehead that made light and noise feel sharp. I skipped Lakshmi's birthday picnic and the school trip, and people started saying I'd turned moody and stuck-up. My uncle said it was "just exam stress, everyone gets it". I believed him for a while and felt stupid for complaining. Then one evening I cried at dinner because the TV was too loud, and Papa put it on mute and said, "Tell me properly." The next week he took me to a doctor, who listened for a long time and asked me to keep a headache diary. We found patterns and made a plan. The headaches didn't vanish overnight, but being believed took half the weight off at once. I phoned Lakshmi and explained. "Why didn't you say?" was all she asked.

qa.q: What did the doctor ask Urmila to keep?
qa.a: A headache diary.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when told it was just exam stress?
qa.a: Urmila felt stupid and misunderstood, doubting whether the pain was real enough to complain about.

qa.q: What helped most, according to Urmila?
qa.a: Being believed and properly checked: Papa listened, the doctor took time and suggested a headache diary, and a plan followed.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt about the missed birthday picnic?
qa.a: Lakshmi may have felt hurt or puzzled at the time, and later wished Urmila had explained.

grounding: Shows a teenager with frequent headaches cancelling plans and being called moody, and the relief of being taken seriously and checked.

When I spoke to him privately, he said he gets headaches most days, and when he told his coach, he was told, "It's nothing, toughen up." He looked close to tears saying it. I told him I believed him and that pain like that deserves a proper check. I've asked staff to let him sit away from the window glare for now.

passage: I used to keep a list in my head of every time Vikas let me down. Skipped my birthday. Left the trek halfway. Replied "k" to a long message about my breakup. I'm Mohit, and I was sure he'd outgrown me. Then last winter I went to his house unannounced and found him lying on the floor with a heat pad on his knee, grey-faced, trying to finish an assignment. He'd had joint pain since he was fifteen, and it had got worse at college. He hadn't told me because he didn't want pity. Everything on my list suddenly looked different. "K" wasn't coldness; it was all he could type that day. Now I ask "good day or bad day?" before making plans, and on bad days I bring snacks and we watch cricket from the floor. He still cancels sometimes. It doesn't sting the way it did.

qa.a: A heat pad.

qa.a: Mohit felt hurt and let down, keeping a list and believing Vikas had outgrown the friendship.

Counsellor's notes, Wednesday
Himani came in today upset about her friend Omkar. They used to study together every evening; now he cancels most plans and answers her in one-word texts. Yesterday he snapped at her in the library, and she cried in the corridor afterwards, wondering what she had done wrong. She mentioned, almost in passing, that he has been living with back pain since a sports injury last year. We talked about how constant pain can drain patience and energy long before it shows on the outside, and how short replies may say more about his day than about her. She decided to ask him directly what helps on bad days rather than guess. She also said she will keep seeing her other friends so she doesn't carry it alone. I'll see her again in two weeks.

passage: Two years after the bike accident, Naveen's neck still burned by evening, and some mornings he couldn't turn his head to check the traffic. He had planned to be a wedding photographer, hauling cameras across Hyderabad every weekend. Now even an hour behind a lens left him flat on the bed. On Saturday Vandana asked if he wanted to go to her cousin's engagement, and he snapped, "Do I look like I can go anywhere?" Then he lay staring at the fan, ashamed. That night he told her the truth: "I'm not angry with you. I'm grieving the job I thought I'd have." Vandana sat beside him. "Then let's plan around the pain, not against it." On Monday they went back to his pain specialist together and agreed on regular physiotherapy. He took on one small portrait shoot a month, with rest breaks written into the schedule.

qa.q: What had Naveen planned to be?
qa.a: A wedding photographer.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling as he lay staring at the fan?
qa.a: He felt ashamed of snapping and full of grief for the photography career he had planned.

qa.q: What steps support Naveen's mood as well as his neck?
qa.a: Being honest with Vandana, returning to his pain specialist for physiotherapy, and pacing his work with one shoot a month and rest breaks.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt when Naveen snapped about the engagement?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt at first, but she listened and offered to plan around the pain with him.

grounding: Shows a young adult with long-lasting pain feeling irritable and grieving a planned life, and finding dignity through honesty, pacing and medical care.

"No. Sorry. I didn't know it was that bad."
"It's always that bad. I just don't announce it."

"That sounds awful."

"Okay. What if we split things differently? I do dishes, you do the grocery orders and the stuff you can do sitting down."

passage: The first year of living with pain, I was mostly angry. I'm Nikita, and I was twenty-three when the ache in my lower back stopped going away after a fall on the hospital stairs. I'd planned night shifts, travel nursing, maybe Canada. Instead I was counting how many minutes I could stand. I snapped at Dhruv when he offered to carry my bag, cried when a friend posted beach photos, and slept badly, which made everything worse. What changed wasn't a miracle. My physiotherapist taught me pacing: work, rest, stretch, before the pain peaked, not after. I told Dhruv the truth, that his help sometimes made me feel useless, and we agreed he'd ask first. I switched to a day-clinic job. Some days are still grey. But I've stopped measuring my life against the one I planned, and I'm less furious at everyone, including myself.

qa.q: What did the physiotherapist teach Nikita?
qa.a: Pacing: work, rest, stretch, before the pain peaked, not after.

qa.q: What did Nikita feel during the first year?
qa.a: Nikita felt mostly angry, grieving the planned life of night shifts and travel nursing.

qa.q: Which changes supported Nikita's mood?
qa.a: Pacing from the physiotherapist, being honest with Dhruv about the help, and moving to a day-clinic job.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt when Nikita snapped about the bag?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt hurt and confused, since he was only trying to help.

grounding: Shows a young adult with long-lasting pain feeling angry and grieving a planned life, and pacing, honesty and proper care supporting mood.

passage: In their village near Nashik, Rekha's knees were worst on cold mornings, after years of grape harvests. Tanvir had learned not to say, "Are you sure it hurts that much?" Instead, each morning he asked, "What would help today?" Some days it was fetching water from the tap. Some days it was reminding her of the exercises the doctor at the taluka hospital had shown her. Some days it was nothing but being left alone with a hot water bottle. On Thursday she barked at him for moving her slippers, and he felt the old sting, then let it pass; he knew the knees were talking. He also knew his own limits. On Sundays he handed the chores to his nephew and played carrom at the panchayat hall for three hours. He came back lighter, and Rekha, who had rested too, laughed at his stories of cheating uncles.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do on Sundays?

passage: In their small flat in Osaka, Yuki had made one rule for herself: ask, don't guess. On bad mornings Noa's back locked so tight that getting out of bed took ten minutes. Yuki used to hover in the doorway, offering tea, heat packs, tips from articles. It made Noa snap, "Stop watching me!" and made Yuki feel useless. Now she asked once: "What would help today?" Today the answer was, "Just the heat pack, and no talking for an hour." Yuki handed it over and went to the kitchen without sulking. The sharpness was pain, not a verdict on her. At noon she laced up her running shoes. "I'm going to the river for an hour. My phone's on." Noa smiled for the first time that day. "Good. Go and breathe for both of us."

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Aditi sat curled on her mother's lap with a runny nose and hot cheeks. "Mumma, carry me like a baby," she whined in a tiny voice, and asked for her old bottle, the one they had put away last year. Her mother flushed. "You're a big girl. Don't talk like that." Aditi's lip wobbled. Nurse Zainab stopped beside them. "Very common. Poorly little ones go back to baby ways for comfort. It fades as they get better." Aditi's mother breathed out, tucked Aditi under her chin, and hummed. Aditi stopped whining.

passage: Naveen had been in bed with flu for three days in their Chennai flat, and his thoughts felt as if they were wading through syrup. When Karthik called about the group project, Naveen listened to his idea of changing the topic and exploded. "Fine, do whatever you want. I don't care about the stupid project!" He hung up and threw the phone onto the blanket. Ten minutes later he was staring at the ceiling, ashamed and worried: what if the others dropped him? What if he failed the term? His mother brought him rasam and found him close to tears. "You're sick, kanna. Everything looks worse right now. Don't settle anything today." The next evening, feeling a little better, he called Karthik back. "Sorry about yesterday. Your topic's actually good. Can we talk properly when I'm back?"

Zeenat

passage: You want to know the worst week of first year? Easy. I'm Ganga, the girl from Kannur who thought she was too grown-up to be homesick. Then in November I got a stomach bug in the hostel. Everyone had gone home for the long weekend. I lay there shivering, too weak to walk to the mess, texting my mother "all fine" because I didn't want her crying on the phone. By the second night I was talking to the ceiling fan and crying about my grandmother's rice gruel. I felt so stupid. Finally I texted Tejas, just "are you on campus?" He came in fifteen minutes with water bottles and bananas, then marched me to the warden, who called the doctor. The lesson? Tell people on day one, not day two. Being sick alone is miserable. Being sick and pretending is worse.

Monday: Worse. She skipped classes. When Francis texted, "missing u in lab, all ok?", she typed "yes" and then deleted it. She typed "actually no, I'm sick" and sent that.
Tuesday: Francis had told the warden on Monday evening, and the warden had taken Alka to the doctor that night. Now Francis sat by her bed copying lab notes while Alka sipped soup and video-called her mother. She still missed home. But the room felt less empty.

passage: Last monsoon I went to work with a fever three days running, because I'd only been at the design studio for four months and was scared of looking flaky. I'm Shalini. Arnab came in feverish again today, second day running, flushed and coughing into his sleeve. He missed a line in the safety checklist that I had to correct, and he snapped at Priyanka when she asked him to repeat a reading. Vishal
